utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please sit down. The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies. And now Ms. Kravetz has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to go back to your testimony of yesterday and start out by clarifying the lines of work that you had as an assistant minister of the MUP in 1998 and 1999. You told us yesterday that you were in charge of alien affairs, travel documents, fire-fighting, and communications; correct? That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. The minister of Internal Affairs with the appropriate internal regulation would entrust assistant ministers, including myself, a certain professional lines of work, and these were, just like you said yourself, administrative affairs, alien affairs, fire-fighting police, and the communications system.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, when you speak about administrative affairs and alien affairs, and yesterday you also said travel documents, are you referring to the administration that in Article 13 of the internal rules of the MUP is called the border police administration for foreigners and administrative affairs, is that the official name of the administration that you were in charge of? Or did it have a different name?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official name of the administration, according to the regulations on internal organisation, was the Administration of Border Affairs for Aliens and Travel Documents. So the administration for border affairs, which I didn't cover, because this involved police work. In my career I was always in charge of operative and administrative tasks; not police tasks. Thus, I was in charge of the duties that I indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who was the head of this administration in 1999? Was there a chief?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the chief of the administration, General Mile Puzovic assigned to the Federal Ministry of Internal Affairs, that post was vacant and the administration was headed by the deputy administration chief, Mr. Petar Dujkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And Mr. Dujkovic, would he report directly to you in matters that concerned administration or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was responsible to the extent that the minister issued me assignments in the administrative area. He was responsible to the assistant minister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how would this reporting take place? Would you meet regularly with Mr. Dujkovic to discuss matters concerning this administration, or would you work with him in another way?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was assistant minister for Internal Affairs, I did not deal with specific cases or matters. I was dealing most of all with systemic matters, primarily organisation and the functional aspect of those administrations for which I was responsible, and helping in the work of the minister. Pero Dujkovic from time to time got in touch with me if we needed to agree on certain assignments, but this was first of all dealing with the organisational aspect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So in matters that did not concern the organisational aspect of that administration, who did he report to?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was responsible to the chief of the department, and the minister for those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. You've also mentioned communications and fire-fighting. Are these two separate administrations?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have the fire-fighting police administration and the communications administration. These are two internal organisational units at the seat of the ministry for Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, you were, in fact, as assistant minister in charge of these three different administrations to the scope of -- or within the scope of work that had been assigned to you with regard to the first?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. I was in charge of these three lines that we discussed for their co-ordination, organisation, proposing the adoption of specific decisions to the minister on the basis of monitoring the situation, and pursuant to the decisions then made by the minister, I would be the one to implement these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And all three of these administrations fell within the RJB; no? They were within the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All three administrations fell under the RJB, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, yesterday you spoke at some length about the role of assistant ministers, and I understand your evidence to be that the role was to help the minister carrying out the tasks or the mandate pertaining to the work of the ministry within the province of work that was -- that they were in charge of specifically, each one of the ministers. Would that be a fair statement of what you understood the role of assistant ministers to be?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I talked about the function of the assistant ministers. Their task primarily was to act on the basis of the minister's decisions because the minister was the only one inherently empowered to organise the service, and then he would task the assistant ministers for certain areas of work. We would be assisting the minister, like I said yesterday, in the making of these decisions, and then later in the implementation of these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And your evidence was that assistant ministers derived their authority from the authority of the minister?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But, sir, the fact that assistant ministers derived their authority from that of the minister does not mean, does it, that assistant ministers, in fact, did not have authority within the ministry, does it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had authority to the extent that it was granted to them by the minister. For example, let's take some matters from my ambit. Let's say communications, I would suggest to the minister that the system be repaired by the purchase of some telephone exchange since the chief of my administration suggested that. After that we would discuss that. If the minister accepted that proposal, then it was up to me. I had the authority to negotiate with the producer, the manufacturer to discuss the price, the type of equipment, and so on and so forth. So I did have the discretion to organise the execution of that assignment and also I had to report back to him on progress.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that after the minister, assistant ministers were, in fact, the most senior members within the MUP, within the structure of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant ministers in any case were of top rank because at the time 1988 and 1989 [as interpreted] we didn't have deputy ministers as compared to the previous period, so in that way this did affect the functioning and the leadership of the ministry itself because the minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic neglected the fact that a deputy minister needed to be appointed. So after the minister, we were the highest ranking or the highest positioned leadership in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you pause a minute. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just would like for Ms. Kravetz to look at line 16 of page 5 of the transcript, these two years.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript records you as saying assistant ministers in any case were the top ranked, "because at the time, 1988 and 1999 [sic] ..." Did you mean to refer to those years 1988 and 1999 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998 and 1999, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have D208 now up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is, sir, a decision setting up the collegium of 4th December, 1998, that you saw yesterday. I'm just waiting for it to come up. Do you recall seeing this yesterday, sir, and going over it with my learned colleague?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see this decision on the setting up of a collegium of the minister of the interior, and I did say that yesterday during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I believe your testimony was that this was the composition of the collegium at that time, and this is December 1998, it included these members?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So we see within this document that there are two members of the DB included, this is Colonel-General Radomir Markovic, and Major-General Nikola Curcic. These were the two members of the state security sector who formed part of the collegium; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both of them were from the state security administration and were members of the minister's collegium pursuant to this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The collegium also included General Obrad Stevanovic. Do you recall what was his position in the years we are concerned with, 1998 and 1999? What was he in charge of?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, General Obrad Stevanovic was in charge of co-ordination, as we refer to it, of the police administration, and for co-ordination of the appropriate organisational units outside of the public security administration. These were the secondary school for Internal Affairs, higher school for Internal Affairs, and the police academy. He was the one who was co-ordinating those particular professional lines of work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the police administration which General Obrad Stevanovic was in charge of, that fell within the RJB, the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police administration was under the public security administration. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what about Petar Zekovic? Major-General Petar Zekovic, what was he in charge of?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Petar Zekovic was in charge of two administrations at the seat of the ministry. That was the general affairs administration and the accommodation administration. He was in charge of the co-ordination of those two administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And that was also within the ambit or scope of the public security sector, these administrations that he was in charge of?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two administrations were also part of the public security administration or department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And the document also lists Major-General Dragan Ilic, the chief of the crime police administration. Crime police administration, that also fell within the RJB; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dragan Ilic was chief of the criminal police administration which was also under the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know why it is that he was included as one of the members of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this was an exceptionally important area in the public security department dealing with very important assignments, primarily crime fighting actions and discovering perpetrators of crimes, it did not have an assistant and that is why in the decision on setting up the collegium of the Ministry of the Interior he was assigned for that. Previously that area was covered by Mr. Radomir Markovic, assistant minister. But since we didn't have an assistant minister for that particular area, then, of course, Dragan Ilic was included in this decision on the setting up of the collegium of the minister of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The last member we see here mentioned is Major-General Branko Djuric, and the chief of the Belgrade SUP, which of course also fell within the RJB, the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said yesterday, all the organisational units in the field, the territorial organisational units, and these are the SUPs, belong to the public security administration as opposed to the territorial organisation of the state security administration where we had certain centres covering specific territories. And they were under the jurisdiction of the state security service. So Branko Djuric as the chief of the Secretariat of Interior in Belgrade was in the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know why he is included as a member of the minister's collegium?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see that this was something that was part of tradition. Since I was working there from the 1970s onwards, the chief of the secretariat of Internal Affairs in Belgrade was always a member of the minister's collegium, first of all because this was a the highest internal organisational unit of the ministry with the most complex problems to deal with in the Republic of Serbia, the most complex crimes and public law and order issues, because it is also the most -- the broadest in its duties. It is always believed that the chief of the secretariat of the interior in Belgrade should always be a member of the minister's collegium. I can say that this was true during the term of office of the minister, or actually the republican secretary Radmilo Bogdanovic. When the post was referred to as ministerial post, it was true during the term of office of Zoran Sokolovic, when he was at that post. And this practice was continued during the term of office of minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, who held the position of head of the Belgrade SUP before Branko Djuric?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the Belgrade SUP before Branko Djuric, General Branko Djuric, was General Petar Zekovic. Petar Zekovic was appointed assistant minister by the government, and Branko Djuric who was the chief of the Internal Affairs department in new Belgrade was appointed as the chief of the Secretariat of the Interior in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And we haven't mentioned Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic who is listed first in this document as assistant minister and chief of the public security department. Now, sir, would you agree with me that within the collegium of the minister, as is set out in this document, General Djordjevic was one of the highest ranking and most senior officers?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chiefs of the public security and state security departments are the highest ranking officers in the ministry. And in this collegium, which is quite normal because while adopting the rules on the internal organisation, the minister set up two basic organisational units, that is the department of state security and the department of public security. And General Djordjevic was the chief of the public security department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see that both he and a General Markovic both hold the rank of Colonel-General, that was, in fact, a highest rank an officer of the MUP could have now within the structure of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Vlastimir Djordjevic and General Radomir Markovic held the highest ranks in the ministry at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to take you now to another document you saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is P357.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And these are the rules -- internal rules and regulations of the MUP. I'm just going to wait for this to come up on the screen. While that is coming up, yesterday you discussed these rules with my learned colleague and you referred to Article 13 of the rules, which establishes 11 organisational units or administrations at the level of the MUP headquarters in Belgrade. Do you recall going over that yesterday with my learned colleague?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to take you to Article 54, which is -- in the English, it's page 42; and in the B/C/S, it's page 45.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So just very briefly, sir the first line here, this is under the section control of organisational units, say the departments shall be controlled by chief of departments. Now, you see that, sir? Article 54.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, sir, you would agree with me that according to the rules of internal organisation of the MUP, the public -- the service department was controlled by the chief of the department which you've told us was Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The public security department was headed by the chief of the department.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in the role of chief of the department, he would have been in charge of the public security department and the organisational unit that formed part of this department, correct, according to these rules?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand that. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll put it -- well, I think you've already answered. What I'm saying is according to these rules, the rules we are looking at, in his role of chief of the department he would have been in charge of the public security department, RJB, and of the organisational units that formed part of that department, the organisational units, in the RJB? Is that clear, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm getting something strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I am sorry, are you having problems with interpretation?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That will be attended to in a minute, sir. Are you hearing me now, are you getting interpretation?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear you. I can hear you now. I can hear the interpreter, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll just repeat my question, it was a very simple question. I was just asking, you've told me earlier that the public security department was headed by the chief of the department, and what I'm asking is based on these rules, the internal rules and regulations of the MUP, the chief of the public security department was in charge of the department of the RJB and of organisational units that formed the department, would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the department or sector heads all organisational units at the seat, and the organisational units in the field and the territory, that is. Those subordinated to him were the chiefs of secretariats. By virtue of the document, the minister delegated powers to the chief of the sector to control and manage these organisational units. However, the minister having appointed a certain number of assistant ministers at the same time narrowed the authority of the chief of the sector. There were four assistant ministers, including myself. We were authorised by the minister to cover our respective lines of duty. In that part of our duties assigned to us by the minister, and we've discussed how it was done yesterday, it was precisely that which limited the authority of the chief of the public sector. Why was that so? Well, by virtue of our rules, the first or immediate superior to assistant ministers is the minister himself. He is also the immediate superior to the heads of organisational units outside the sectors, such as the schools and the director of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think we got your position on that yesterday, and it wasn't my intention to repeat all of that evidence. I was just asking a very specific question, and you've given your answer to that question. So I'm sorry, I'm going to interrupt you there just so we can move on. Sir, these rule we are looking at, they apply to the work of the ministry in the entire territory of Serbia; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to look at another document. This is D396. If we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday you looked at a decision which appointed General Djordjevic as acting head of the RJB. This is the decision that appoints him as head of the public security department, and it's headed 27th January, 1998. I'll give you a minute to look at that.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And we see this is, well, as I've stated, dated January 1998. You would agree with me, sir, based on the regulations we saw and on this decision that in order for Mr. Djordjevic to cease in the exercises of his functions or powers as chief of the RJB, MUP Minister Stojiljkovic would have to formally divest him of his powers; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister was authorised to issue an appropriate decision and to assign people to different positions including the chief of the sector. So there's nothing wrong with this. He appointed him as of the 1st of February of that year to that position. We were all surprised a bit that up until that time he was only acting chief of the public security sector, and as such could not exercise his functions properly. I spoke frequently at the minister collegium meetings, he was just an announcer at such meetings, so to say. He would simply give the floor to speakers. But the weight of his words and authority was not such because he was only acting chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My question was more specific, sir. You've told us yesterday during the course of your evidence that Mr. Djordjevic remained in the position of chief of the public security department in 1998 and 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He remained in that position in both 1998 and 1999, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So just going back to my question, isn't it true, sir, that in those years as of his appointment, he was never, and I'm talking about Mr. Djordjevic, officially divested of his powers of minister? That did not happen in 1998 or in 1999?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I did not understand your question fully, but perhaps I can answer it this way: Of course --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Let me state it again. In 1998 or in 1999, did -- at any time did the minister issue a decision like the one we are seeing now officially stating that Mr. Djordjevic ceased in the function of head of the public security department? Did that happen in either of those two years, based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that did not take place during 1998 or 1999. In other words, he remained chief of the public security sector. There were no decisions removing him from that position of his.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want to now go back to the collegium. We were looking at D208.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe if we could have it back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke at length about the MUP collegiums, the collegiums of the minister of the MUP; do you recall answering some questions from my learned colleague in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said, sir, that one of the ways in which the ministry was run was through meetings of the collegium of the MUP minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You regularly attended those meetings?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, for the most part. Perhaps sometimes I was in the field, but I attended most of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said these meetings took place in 1998, throughout 1998?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they were held throughout all of 1998. For a while, the minister, as far as I recall, he was appointed after General Stojicic's murder. There was an interim period of one or two months during which there were no collegium meetings of the minister of the interior. What there was, was the collegium of the chief of the public security sector. When the minister was elected to his position on the 4th of June, he assigned duties to the assistant ministers, and at some point in time the meetings of the collegium of minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic began taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when was General Stojicic murdered; do you recall? Was that in 1998?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was in 1997. 1997, on the 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this interim period of one or two months that you are referring to when there were no collegium meetings, this would be prior to the 4th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the 4th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said in relation to 1999 that you had collegiums during the war, though the circumstances were more difficult; correct? That was your evidence, that these meetings continued to be -- take place during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. During the war the meetings of the minister's collegium were held in a number of locations and, of course, under much more difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in 1998 with what frequency were these meetings held? As of the 4th of June when they were resumed, how often would the collegium of the minister meet?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the minister's collegium meetings, as a rule, were held every week, basically every Tuesday, or sometimes on another day depending on the obligations of the minister. Such collegium meetings were basically held every week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was that also the practice in 1999?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that practice continued in 1999, but it wasn't always on the same day because we had our own obligations and issues to resolve that had to do with bombing campaign. But for the most part, it resumed the same way -- it was resumed the same way in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: These meetings were generally presided by the MUP minister Stojiljkovic? He chaired the meetings?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those meetings were presided solely by the minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. In his absence, there were no collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you spoke about the other attendees at these meetings, and at transcript page 14030 you said: "In addition to the chief of the public security sector, also the chief of the state security sector was to be present as well as his assistant, another assistant minister, in fact, Nikola Curcic, who was otherwise a director of the security institute." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you were shown this document, this document dated 4th of December, 1998, which we have on the screen, you were asked by my learned colleague - this is the next page, 14031: "Can you tell us what the minister's collegium actually looked like and how it worked once this 4th of December decision was issued?" And you said: "Once this decision was issued, the work of the collegium, in fact, continued on as before." And you went on to explain: "At the collegium meeting, the minister asked reports to be submitted by chiefs of administration, they did so, they also proposed various measures. Then assistant ministers and the sector chief would also take the floor, and at the end the minister would issue conclusions." Do you recall saying that, sir, yesterday?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you went on to say -- and this is at the bottom of 14031 and starts on the next page. You were asked: "You said that chiefs of administration attended these meetings, but can you tell us which particular sector these administrations belonged to?" And you said: "Well, you see that it is stated here that the collegium is composed of nine members, in actual fact; however, the collegium never met if this particular composition." And then you went on to say: "Rather, the previous practice was adhered to, whereby all chiefs of administrations would attend." And you said: "Chiefs of administration of state security never attended these meetings." And you were asked: "This was the way of proceeding at the collegium of the minister following the 4th of December, 1998. Did it prevail up to the end of the war in 1999?" And you said: "Yes, that's right." Do you recall giving that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not what I said. There must have been a mistake made. The chief of the state security sector as of the 4th of December, 1998, always attended collegium meetings. Both the chief and his deputy. The way I understood you now was that I said that the chief of the state security sector never attended those meetings. As a matter of fact, I was saying that until the 4th of December when the collegium was established, there was no one from the state security sector attending those meetings because Mr. Jovica Stanisic simply did not attend those collegium meetings. After the 4th of December, after the minister issued the decision, as of that moment on, Mr. Radomir Markovic, the chief of the state security sector and his deputy, Mr. Nikola Curcic, did attend minister's collegium meetings. I also said that there were also chiefs of administrations in attendance, always, representing all of the organisational units at the seat of the ministry, as it had been the practice in 1998. This decision was not implemented in the sense that the nine members of the collegium should meet at collegium meetings. What actually happened was that the collegium meetings were attended by the chiefs of administrations. That is to say, administrations from the public security sector. Never were there any heads of administrations from the state security sector in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, sir. Now, was -- just to continue on the topic of these meetings, was there an agenda set beforehand regarding what a meeting would -- what you would be dealing with at a meeting? Or did you just follow-up from previous staff that had been assigned at the previous meeting, or how did that work?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never received the agenda. This represented standard mode of operation. We also knew that the chiefs of administrations were there to submit their reports having analysed the security situation in their respective areas. Based on such analyses, they also pointed out the problems and proposed measures to overcome them. Next, the assistant ministers and the chief of the -- the chiefs of the public and state security sectors put forth appropriate proposals and suggestions. Based on all that, at the end the minister drew conclusions and assigned the focal tasks for the forthcoming period. Based on those focal tasks, minutes were made by the chief of the analysis administration, Mr. Krstic. Those minutes would then, in turn, be distributed to all those in attendance. And everyone had to abide by those conclusions. At the following collegium meeting, they were expected to submit reports on what they had done concerning those. Let us understand each other. At collegium meetings, the so-called petty issues were not paid much attention. At that level, appropriate security policies were decided upon at the level of the ministry. Thus, directing all organisational units and forces in the field. We couldn't, of course, deal with individual cases because there were hundreds and thousands of them. We could only indicate trends, patterns, based on which we could draw conclusions and exercise our functions by doing so and following up. To conclude, there was no specific agenda before any collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you didn't attend a collegium meeting, would you receive copies of the minutes to inform yourself of what had transpired at the previous collegium meeting, or what had been decided and which staff had been assigned?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we always received them irrespective of whether we attended those meetings, because after all, we had to follow it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you still have a copy, sir, of the minutes of these collegiums that you attended in 1998 and 1999 in your personal archives?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't. Everything I had was in the safe in the ministry. When I retired, I had to hand it all over. It was, of course, forbidden to take such minutes and documents out of the ministry. It was -- they were secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you've told us you retired in 2000, in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I left towards the end of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So the copies of your minutes of these meetings would still be in the ministry, if I understand you correctly? Once you left, that's where they are kept, in the archive of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. They should be in the ministry. And perhaps the analysis department has copies. However, my copies remained with the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And that would have also been the case of the copies received by other assistant ministers once they'd left office, they would have had to return them and hand them over to the archive of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. There could be a small problem though because the Ministry of the Interior was bombed on the 3rd of April. The building of the ministry was destroyed. In all likelihood, a great many documents were thus destroyed. For example, all of my personal documentation was destroyed. Now I basically have no documents at all at home regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on, sir, yesterday you were speaking about the topics discussed at these collegiums, and you said that at the beginning or end of the collegiums, MUP minister Stojiljkovic normally gave a brief overview of the situation of Serbia with particular -- and a security situation of Serbia with particular emphasis on Kosovo. And this was at transcript page 14031. Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you also said, and this is at transcript page 14033, that the security situation in Kosovo in mid-1998 was an extremely complex and difficult situation; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In mid-1998 it was exceptionally complex, the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija, that is. I also said that almost 50 per cent of the territory was blocked by the terrorists. There was no freedom of movement. We had numerous incidents, such as terrorist attacks on policemen, soldiers. There were many casualties among the police and army. We had non-stop terrorist provocations. Our buildings were being attacked. The buildings of the ministry and of the army. People were building kidnapped, Serbs and Albanians. Those Albanians loyal to the state of Serbia. Next there were many murders of Serbs, non-Albanians, and even Albanians loyal to the state of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also said that our economy, society, and the state there, was basically paralysed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was just asking you confirm this one statement you made yesterday. We do have your evidence you gave yesterday on this topic. So you would agree with me, sir, that given that the situation in Kosovo in mid-1998 was, as you've put it, extremely -- exceptionally complex, it was always the focus of attention at collegium meetings of the MUP ministry?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the priorities at the collegium ministry sessions was the situation in Kosmet. But the situation in Kosmet, generally speaking, meant that the minister was in contact with the Chief of Staff in Kosmet who had information. The minister also had information, on the other hand, from politicians who also were there, and he would then give a brief overview without going much into detail. For example, that such and such a road was unblocked or such and such a settlement. Other details were not discussed at the collegium. This would always be done by the minister of Internal Affairs. He would be the one who would give us these kind of brief pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I didn't mean to interrupt you, sir, just to move on in my question. You would agree with me, sir, that Kosovo was, in fact, the most important security-related situation in which the RJB was involved in, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was extremely important. However, the collegium ministry -- the ministry collegium would receive requests for logistical support, for police forces that were in Kosmet. Requests would be for vehicles, weapons, and so on. As for the material and financial services or general services, they also had some logistical tasks. We would receive requests for the reinforcement of certain units, the sending of additional forces, or to relieve forces that were already there. This was done by the police administration. These questions were constantly on the agenda because there was no other way for us to monitor the current situation in Kosmet. We would put all of our efforts to help those people and our organisational units and the police units that were in Kosovo fighting terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I had asked you about 1998. You would agree with me, sir, that Kosovo remained the most important security-related situation in which the RJB was involved in 1999?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. This was one of the urgent matters that we had to deal with. Yesterday I did say, though, that the minister in 1998 formed the ministry staff for anti-terrorist actions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. We will get to that in a minute, so -- just so we don't get ahead of ourselves. We will turn to that in a minute. Sir, in 1998, the RJB had approximately 14.000 MUP personnel deployed in Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't confirm that information because I don't remember, and I wasn't really involved in those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough. Now, you've told us, sir, that at collegium meetings of the MUP minister, you would deal with logistical tasks that concerned organisational units deployed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the ministry collegium primarily discussed logistical issues and ways to assist our forces in Kosmet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you dealt with the procurement of equipment for the units that were on the ground; correct?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you also said today that you would receive requests on reinforcement of units, and that was another issue you dealt with, the reinforcement of units that were on the ground?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We always received requests to relieve a unit or send a unit to Kosmet. These were mostly relating to the PJP units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said just a moment ago that this was done by the police administration at the meetings of the minister. That would have been General Stevanovic who was representing the police administration? Was he the one who was making these requests for relief of units and procurement of equipment?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that before. Obrad Stevanovic was assistant minister because there was no chief of the police administration at the time, then Colonel Aleksic was deputy chief of the police administration and in that capacity attended the collegium meetings. I forgot to say that in the annex to the minister's decision forming the collegium, Mr. Ljubo Aleksic is not mentioned at all. This is why I said that it was a question of what sort of a list that was. Obrad Stevanovic did not send such requests. The requests for replenishment of units were sent by the staff, the Ministry of Internal Affairs in Kosovo to the administration, and then the administration in turn carried out that other, let me put it that way, logistical technical aspect of the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to make sure I understand your evidence, when you say that you were dealing with these requests at the minister's collegium, you were dealing with requests that came from the MUP staff, or you were dealing with requests that were being presented by Colonel Aleksic, the deputy chief? Or maybe neither of these two.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Requests were not sent directly to the minister's collegium. Requests were sent by the very nature of things to the police administration because the police administration deals with all the uniformed persons in the ministry. Of course, police stations and other organisational units of the police. So the police administration would receive requests as to what had to be done. They would then suggest that to the minister. The minister would then make the appropriate decision on the engagement of that unit, and then they would just send those units to Kosmet. I don't know if I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say the police administration would receive the requests and then suggest that to the minister, was that done at the collegium?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were told to the minister. They were also made at the collegium so that that would enter the minutes. For example, that a certain unit had to be sent to Kosovo so that the minister would have a record of which unit would need to be sent in order to relieve units that were already there, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say they were told to the minister, who told the minister? That's what I'm trying to understand about these requests at the collegium.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief or the deputy chief of the administration would make the requests or the proposals at the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you are speaking of General Stevanovic or Mr. Aleksic who you've referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time Mr. Stevanovic was not at the collegium sessions, as far as I recall. This was something that Mr. Aleksic did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. So you spoke about dealing with reinforcements of units and relieving units in the field. You would also discuss then -- are you okay, sir? Yes.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You would also discuss the rotation of units; no? Which units would be sent, which units would be brought back out of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we would receive requests from the staff and then we would act pursuant to those requests and assist them to receive appropriate forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us earlier today that another matter that was discussed and that you decided at these meetings were appropriate security policies with respect to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. I didn't say that at all. What sort of security policies?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If you give me just a second, you say: "Let us understand each other. At collegium meetings the so-called petty issues were not paid much attention. At that level appropriate security policies were decided upon at the level of the ministry. Thus, directing all organisation of units and forces in the field." And this is at page 20 starting at line 8. Do you recall saying that, sir? This was another matter that you discussed security policies, and this was decided at the level of these collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Let me give you some specific examples. Since we were under sanctions, then there was the observation that goods subject to excise taxes were being smuggled. The government then put the question to the minister about what was being done in that area. Then the minister came to the collegium meeting and instructed the services how and what to deal with that. This meant that we had to gather all the necessary information, we had to make a security analysis and on the basis of that apply adequate or change our conduct adequately. We made our own analysis from the secretariat and the information on the ground. We analysed the situation at the ministry, and then together with authorised state organs, got in touch with the judicial organs and suggested to the minister to launch appropriate actions. Well, maybe doesn't make much sense, but I can list which actions were involved. Then once an action is initiated, then plans are made which facilities and forces are needed to deal with that particular problem. This is how this was done. We didn't actually review any individual cases, for example, such and such a person hit such and such a person or this and that. I'm just talking about the general occurrence of certain things that were happening. This is what we were looking at because the ministry was there in order to direct overall potentials and capacities for action in the field, so I was talking more in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you would also discuss, sir, any changes in the tactics of the work of the police in Kosovo; no?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Changes of tactics? This question was never put at the minister's collegium. What change of tactics? We never dealt with anything like that. I'm hearing of that for the first time, changes of tactics in Kosmet. That question was never looked at or dealt with at sessions of the minister's collegium.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But, sir, you've told us you started meeting again as of 4th of June -- or in June of 1998. You would have discussed at the level of the collegium of the ministry that the MUP was stepping up its actions in Kosovo? No? That would have been something that would have been discussed at that level, that you planned to step up.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was never discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that you would -- the fact that the MUP was about to engage in a large-scale offensive in Kosovo against the KLA together with the VJ, that was not a matter that was discussed at the level of the collegium of the minister in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a number of times which questions were tabled. We practically, other than logistics, the questions that I mentioned earlier, could not discuss the actions of the police because we didn't have any experts for that part of the work at the collegium. That was on the one hand. On the other hand, we didn't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you are saying you did not have information during the summer of 1998 that the MUP was about to engage in a large-scale offensive against the KLA in Kosovo with the VJ? You didn't have that information at the level of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is quite a different question altogether. The information we had was that a state plan was made or that was being prepared, that this plan was drafted by the army, that it was engaging in the fight against terrorists. There was some global state plan. We were told this but we never discussed that plan at the level of the ministry or at the level of the minister's collegium. I never saw that plan and I was a member of the collegium, so I would have had to see or should have seen this plan. Thus, it was said that a state plan was drafted, or rather, a global plan, as far as I can remember. But we did not review it, and I never saw it. And I was a member of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I started asking you whether you would discuss at the collegiums any changes in the tactics of the police in Kosovo. Now, based on this answer you've just given, is it correct, sir, that, in fact, at the level of the collegium in Belgrade, you were discussing the fact that the MUP was about to engage in a large-scale offensive against the KLA together with the VJ? That is something the collegium at the level of the ministry in Belgrade was fully aware of and you were discussing? I'm not asking whether you saw the plan; I'm asking whether this was something that you were discussing at the collegium.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, allow me to repeat what I said earlier. It's not that I didn't see the plan, but at the minister's collegium this was not discussed at all. I think that I'm quite clear in this now. The minister's collegium did not discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Maybe we are talking at cross purposes here. I'm asking you a very specific question. I'm asking whether at the level of the ministry in the summer of 1998 you discussed the fact of the -- at the level of the collegium of the minister, you discussed the fact that the MUP was about to engage in a large-scale offensive against the KLA together with the VJ? That's what I'm asking. Was this a matter of discussion? I'm putting to you that it was, that this was something that was discussed at the level of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state that this was not discussed at the level of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At all? You never spoke about the fact that operations were going to be stepped up in Kosovo in the summer of 1998? Never discussed that at all?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was no discussion about the intensification of activities. We received information that some state plan had been devised which provides for the engagement of the police and the army in the fight against terrorists, but nothing was worked out, discussed, or planned in any way about the way in which these anti-terrorist activities would be planned at our end. We did have the appropriate staff, and that staff was obliged in co-operation with the military to draft plans and to work on the suppression of terrorism in Kosmet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you were, you've told us already, receiving requests from the ground, from the MUP staff from the police administration concerning logistics, no, and the reinforcements of units?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that this happened during the summer of 1998 you received such requests? And by you, I'm talking about the collegium.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In the course of the summer. Summer of 1998. From what I can recall, sometime in July until the end of September or October these requests for the replacement of units were quite pronounced. Yes, during the summer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you would have also been aware of the number of units that were being sent down based on these requests? You knew which units and the number of units that were going down to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did know, but I really cannot say that now. It's been awhile since then, so I cannot really remember. It was known, though, they --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, just finish your answer, sir. I wasn't asking you for specific numbers. I was just asking whether at the level of the collegium you would have known that.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew about the requests and the number being requested, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And so you would have also known at the level of the collegium that there was an intensification of police activities and that additional units were being sent down given that you were dealing with these requests?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can ask -- well, I said earlier that the minister gave us brief overviews at the minister's collegium because, like I said, he received those reports both from the staff and the state security, primarily from the staff. And he knew more or less -- actually, not more or less, but he knew that such and such a road - what do I know - the Pec-Pristina Road was unblocked, that work was being done, that the intensity had increased. As to what extent you would understand that we knew, yes, on the basis of a brief report by the minister. He would always give some kind of evaluation or assessment and inform us briefly, but we did not discuss anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, it's two minutes before the break, but I would prefer to interrupt now before I move onto another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well adjourn now and resume at just after ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday and today you said that in 1998 and 1999, and I'm quoting your testimony from yesterday at transcript page 14040: "We never discussed planning and the conduct of anti-terrorist activities at the collegium sessions, nor did we receive any reports about the implemented activities." That was your position yesterday, correct, which you've repeated today?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In fact, yesterday at transcript page 14054, you said: "Not once during the war did we discuss planning, organising, or implementation of anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija." And you also said -- repeated that you did not receive any reports on that. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We've been focusing so far in 1998. Sir, in 1999, somewhere in the middle February 1999, do you recall attending a meeting of the MUP collegium where a plan to be developed for the eventuality of the entry of NATO forces to Kosovo was discussed?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said in February 1999, such a collegium meeting, or rather, I did not attend such a collegium meeting. I don't know that it was ever held, and I don't know that such a plan was discussed during one such meeting. Such a collegium meeting with that agenda was not held, or rather, I definitely did not attend such a collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You don't recall any meeting where you discussed measures to be taken by RJB units in Kosovo in preparation for a NATO attack? You don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. I would definitely remember such a thing because it is an important topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, I want --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I definitely did not attend such a collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I want to show you a document. Maybe this refreshes your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is P1509 MFI. If we could have that up on the screen. And I want page 37 in the English, and in the B/C/S this is page 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And sir, what we are going to see on the screen is a note-book of General Obrad Stevanovic. It's a handwritten note-book. And it might be a bit difficult for you to read on that screen, so I'm going to go ahead and read to you some of the points that are raised at this meeting just to see if this refreshes your memory about this meeting. The date, as indicated here in this note-book, is 14 February 1999. It's a MUP collegium meeting, and among the attendees are the minister, then it says, Rodja. Rodja was Mr. Djordjevic, correct, that's how he was known?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Rade. That would have been Mr. Markovic?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And then there's Misic, Djuric, Ilic, someone by the name of Danilo, and then it says, myself. And under the heading "The Minister," it says: "A plan should be developed for the eventuality of the entry of NATO forces. Do you see that, sir? It's the second bullet point after the heading, "The minister." And then he goes on to say: "Kosovo must not be surrendered at any cost, because no one will be able to take it back." Further down in the page the minister says --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here. I don't see what you've just read out. First of all, I don't understand whose handwriting is, whose notes are these?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, this is the --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who drafted this document? What is this? Are these minutes or what? Could I be told that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned this when I called the document. This is the note-book of handwritten notes of General Obrad Stevanovic. And I'm putting to you simply to see if it refreshes your memory of having attended this meeting and the topics discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my learned colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, so I'm reading out to you the notes General Stevanovic made of this meeting. He records you as one of the attendees, and it's a meeting that was held on the 14th of February. And as I mentioned, the reason I'm reading it out is I understand that the copy, as you see it on the screen, is going to be a difficult to read. So further down the page the minister says: "If they start strikes, we shall have to destroy the terrorists with lightening speed." And turning the page in the English, he is recorded as saying: "We must avoid a civil war (RPO police stations as noted)." Sir, does this refresh your recollection of having attended a meeting in mid-February of the minister's collegium where a plan to be developed in the eventuality of an attack by NATO was discussed and where these other topics was discussed? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely do not. These things somebody wrote are absolutely untrue. I can't recognise this handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And sir, you maintain that at the level of the collegium of the minister, you never discussed any sort of plans involving preparations for or plans of activities to be undertaken by the RJB in preparation of the NATO offensive? That is your position; you don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I don't recall it. Such a collegium meeting was never held. I don't know who wrote this with these topics. I know of no such collegium meeting. If this is a note pad of Mr. Stevanovic, these may have been his preparatory notes for something. In any case, there was no collegium meeting with these topics, with these stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, in the middle February 1999 that the RJB was preparing a plan for its units down in the field in Kosovo that would be carried out or launched once the NATO attack began, or in the eventuality that a NATO attack was carried out? Were you aware that that was being planned?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such a plan. In all the meetings I attended in the public security sector, such a plan was not mentioned or created. It simply did not exist at the level of the public security sector. I attended those meetings, but we did not make up any plans to prevent the forces of the NATO Alliance in case of their attack on our country. And it's not a police task to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that you did not even hear a reference to the fact that the RJB was preparing itself for the possibility of a NATO attack and was preparing its units in the field? You didn't even hear that -- a reference at meetings that there was such a plan? I'm not asking if you were personally involved in preparing it. I'm asking whether if you don't even recall hearing about this at meetings.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear of such a plan. Only on one occasion I think I saw a dispatch in which the minister issued some such measures. He frequently did so without our knowledge, but I never heard of the existence of such a plan, and I never participated in it. Whatever this gentleman wrote has nothing to do with anything. It's not true. I don't even believe it is Obrad Stevanovic's diary. However, I can't recognise the handwriting, therefore, I can't say anything with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we have gone far enough to allow the witness to give his reaction. Now, Mr. Djurdjic, your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a procedural objection concerning the use of this document. It is for the third time that the Prosecutor made use of it. I was interrupted on all three occasions because these references were presented without providing the author of the document and what the document was about. Finally, Ms. Kravetz for the first time stated what it is. I think it is -- this document was supposed to be used for the second time when the accused Djordjevic under different circumstances. The existence of this diary was denied by the witness, and the Prosecutor dropped that particular witness. The Chamber allowed the document to be used as an MFI'd document, rather than putting it to any witnesses about what someone wrote in it. I believe now Ms. Kravetz is -- seems to be finished with it; otherwise, I would have asked for the witness to take his headphones off. I believe you, Your Honours, propose that it be MFI'd to have a clear idea of what questions were to be put to the witness concerning this document, and I believe the OTP has now gone too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification. It has been put to more than one witness. As far as I recall, although I haven't checked, no witnesses yet identified or accepted it, so it is not an exhibit, and that's as far as it can be taken by Ms. Kravetz, unless a witness does accept the correctness of the contents of the document at some time. Carry on, please, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have one more page I want to show of this document, and I'm referring to it for the purpose of trying to refresh the witness's recollection on the issues that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you just said in all the meetings that you attended in the public security sector, such a plan was not mentioned or created. Sir, do you recall attending a meeting where finishing touches for a plan for a broad anti-terrorist operation between -- with the MUP involving the MUP and the Pristina Corps was discussed? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never attended such a meeting. Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is page 40 in the English, and it's page 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this is a collegium of -- it's dated 16th of February, and it's headed collegium of the chief of the public security sector. And we see the note there that's been made in this note-book. It says, number 1: "In accordance with orders from earlier meetings, measures are being taken for an action in case of air-strikes or entry by force of NATO troops in KiM." That's at the top of the page number 1. And then it says: "Together with the Pristina Corps, the finishing touches are being put to the plan for a broad anti-terrorist operation in the period between the possible air-strikes and the entry of ground forces." And then is says: "Sending all OPJP, PJP, detachments." Does that refresh your recollection, sir, that these matters were being discussed at the level of the collegium of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could understand you seem to have said a moment ago that this was in February 1999. Now you also said that there was a collegium meeting of the public security sector. I assert that there was no collegium of the public security sector. I said a number of times that there was the minister's collegium. It's a different matter than that at that collegium the public security sector was mostly discussed. The collegium of the public security sector would entail that the chief of the public security sector presided over such a collegium. Such collegiums did not exist. Why would there be any? If we had the minister's collegium where all assistants were present --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: My question was very specific. I'm just asking you whether this passage that I read out to you refreshes your recollection that this matters, the fact that there was preparations made for a plan that was going to be carried out once NATO forces attacked, whether this refreshes your recollection that these matters were being discussed in -- at the level of the public security sector. So I'm actually just looking for a yes or no, does it refresh your recollection or not?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no. If you want me to be brief, then the answer is no. And I've just tried to explain some of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to show you another document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is P85. If we could have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this, sir, the document we'll have up on the screen are the minutes of the meeting of the Pristina MUP staff which you've referred to. And I just want to read out a passage. This is the -- these are the minutes of a meeting held on the 17th of February, 1999, and we see among the attendees are Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic; the public security department chief, Colonel Vlastimir Djordjevic; we also have the RDB head there, General Markovic; and then General Stevanovic and other members of the staff; and the heads of SUPs and of units down in Kosovo. Do you see that, sir, that these persons are there among the attendees?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would like to direct your attention to somewhere towards the bottom off the page. It's General Sreten Lukic who is speaking here, and he says -- and this is a sentence starting by, "a plan of the RJB." He says: "A plan of the RJB has been worked out to prevent and thwart the entry of NATO troops into our territory. The staff plans when it is ordered to carry out three mopping up operations in the Podujevo, Dragobilja, and Drenica areas, and has allotted around 4.000 policemen, around 70 policemen of the operative group, and around 900 police reservists. On Saturday, 20 February of 1999, a meeting of the staff will be held with police detachment unit commanders for further consultations about their engagement." Do you see that, sir, that passage that I just read out?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you, sir, at the time, we are talking mid-February, 1999, know about this plan of the RJB to launch these actions which are being referred to here in this meeting that involves all senior members of the RJB and also the RDB for that matter? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood, this meeting was supposed to be held in Kosovo at the staff in Pristina. In any case, I did not hear of it, and I did not see any minutes such as these. I absolutely knew of no plan of the public security sector to prevent the entry of NATO troops into our country. It is stated here a plan of the public security sector, but this needn't necessarily mean that the plan was discussed at the level of the minister's collegium, and that we talked about it. I don't know of such a plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we see from the minutes here that other members of the collegium -- we've gone through all the list of members who were in attendance, General Djordjevic and Markovic, also the minister and General Stevanovic. Were you not aware, sir, that all these senior members of the ministry had travelled down to Pristina at the time and attended this meeting where this plan that was going to be launched was discussed? This was not something that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall it after this many years, but I don't think I was aware of it. It was not the first time that the minister with a number of his assistants attended some meetings, but that didn't necessarily mean that I was aware of them going there discussing any issues. I wasn't aware of this meeting, and I wasn't aware of the plan. Finally, I had my own tasks on which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you've told us, sir, that the minister at the start of these collegium minutes, he would update other members about the security situation in Kosovo and events there. Are you saying, sir, that after the minister and other members of the collegium returned from this meeting in Pristina, there was no mention or reference made at the collegium about the fact that this meeting had taken place and the matters discussed there?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't necessarily need to advise us of that meeting and of his presence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you are saying you heard nothing about it?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to draw your attention to page 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could see that both in the English and the B/C/S. I believe in the Serbian, it's somewhere towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is the same document, we are still within the minutes of this meeting, and this is minister Stojiljkovic who is speaking here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly read slowly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We see somewhere, it's the eighth bullet point, we see the minister saying: "Tell the RPO and the people that a civil war must be avoided at all cost, but that in case of a conflict, not women and children should be killed, only the aggressor." Do you see that entry, sir? I think it's somewhere towards the bottom of your page from what I'm seeing in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this indicate to the RPO and the citizens? Because I don't see here it being under item 8. I just see bullet points here. You said item 8; I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, I said -- maybe it's just a problem of the translation. Eighth bullet point is what I was referring to. So I take it you've found the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that is "tell the RPO and the people that a civil war must be avoided at all costs." Is that what you are referring to? I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in the note-book I had shown you earlier of notes taken by General Stevanovic at the meeting of 14th of February --

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please just, just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Let me finish my question. In that note-book we saw where we saw the notes of a meeting on the 14th of February, we saw that under the topics that Minister Stojiljkovic had raised was also the fact where it said, "we must avoid a civilian war (RPO)." Do you remember I showed you that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall that now, but I would kindly ask to be told what the RPO is. RPO. There were no such organisational forms at the ministry. I don't know what it is. Tell the RPO and the citizens that a civil war must be avoided at all costs. Could you please make it a little bit more accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Based on the evidence we've heard here in this trial, RPO is an acronym that was used for reserve police squads. Do you have any knowledge of that? Have you heard about that before, or is this the first time that you see that?

utterances.speaker: STOJAN MISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what that means, the reserve police squads. We, Madam Prosecutor, did not have such reserve police squads. If I understood correctly what you've said, reserve police squads. We did have the reserve forces in the detachments of the PJP, but detachments or squads as independent squads of reserve police, we didn't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have an objection to what Ms. Kravetz said because she said that the way it's being used here. I have an objection to the interpretation. RPO are not reserve police squads, but they are reserve police sections or squads. I don't know how the interpreters are going to translate that. Well, section. Now, I think we are having a problem as far as that is concerned. I'm not going to continue with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
